images.fact: Started in Italian and French royal courts. Dancers train at a barre and dance on their toes "en pointe".
Born in the 1880s in Buenos Aires and Montevideo. Known for close holds and sharp, dramatic moves.
From Andalusia in southern Spain, with stamping feet, clapping, guitar and frilled dresses.
A Māori challenge dance with stamping, chanting and tongue-poking. The All Blacks do one before rugby matches.
Arms stay still while the feet do fast, precise steps. Made world-famous by Riverdance in 1994.
A Hawaiian dance where hand movements tell a story, often with chanting or ukulele.
Focuses on hip and stomach movements. Often performed with jingling coin belts.
Started in the Bronx in the 1970s. Breaking became an Olympic sport at Paris 2024.
Dancers wear shoes with metal plates, so their feet become a drum.
A high-kicking, skirt-swishing dance from 1840s Paris, made famous by the Moulin Rouge.
Dancers bend backwards under a bar that gets lower each round: "How low can you go?"
Two dancers inside a lion costume bring good luck, especially at Lunar New Year.
A team holds up a long dragon on poles and makes it snake around. Seen at Lunar New Year.
Dancers weave ribbons around a tall pole to celebrate spring and midsummer.
Everyone does the same steps in rows, usually to country music, with no partner needed.
Done in kilts at Highland Games. The Sword Dance is danced over two crossed swords.
English folk dancers in white, with bells on their legs, waving hankies or clashing sticks.
A spiritual Sufi ceremony where dancers spin for a long time in white robes as a form of prayer.
One of India's oldest classical dances, from Tamil Nadu. Hand gestures and facial expressions tell stories.
A fast partner dance mixing Cuban rhythms, popularised in New York in the 1960s–70s.
A figure skating event where a couple dance together on ice. It's been an Olympic sport since 1976.
Started at US college sports games. Now includes stunts, lifts and tumbling.
Dancers in hanbok dresses use painted fans to make flower and wave shapes.
Dancers swirl huge, colourful skirts. The Mexican Hat Dance is the most famous one.
Brazil's national dance, the star of the Rio de Janeiro Carnival, with feathers and sequins.
Part dance, part martial art, created by enslaved Africans in Brazil. Played in a circle to music.
An energetic harvest dance from Punjab with bright clothes, bouncing shoulders and the dhol drum.
A gliding ballroom dance in 3/4 time ("ONE-two-three") that swept Vienna in the 1800s.
Ukraine's national dance, with high jumps, splits and squatting kicks.
Aboriginal Australian dances tell Dreaming stories, often with ochre body paint and clapsticks.
Māori performers swing balls on cords in rhythm. It was once used to train hand strength and flexibility.
Spins and inverted holds on a vertical pole. Now a competitive fitness sport.
Four couples in a square follow instructions shouted by a "caller", like "swing your partner".
Dancers hop between two bamboo poles that are clapped together, inspired by the tikling bird.
Classical dance-drama from Kerala. Performers wear green face make-up and huge headdresses, and can take hours to get ready.
A circle of up to 100 men chant "cak-cak-cak" to act out the Ramayana epic, often at sunset.
Young Maasai warriors take turns jumping straight up as high as they can while the others chant.
Native American gatherings with drumming and dance contests. Fancy dancers wear colourful feathered regalia.
Japanese summer festival dance in honour of ancestors, done in yukata or kimono, often in a big circle.
Dancers do high stamping kicks to drums, traditionally with shields and animal-skin costumes.
Men in lederhosen jump, stamp and slap their thighs, knees and shoe soles in rhythm.
Created by gold miners who could not talk while working, so they slapped and stamped their rubber boots to send messages.
Buddhist monks dance in huge painted masks of gods and demons at monastery festivals to scare away evil.
Dancers spin, toss and catch a long knife with both ends on fire. There is a world championship for it in Hawaii.
Danced in big circles over the nine nights of the Navratri festival, often in mirrored, colourful skirts. Dandiya is the version with sticks.
A line dance done at weddings, with dancers linked by hands or shoulders stamping the ground together.
Dancers in golden crowns copy the heavenly dancers carved on the walls of Angkor Wat, bending their fingers far back.
Men kneel in a tight row and clap, slap their chests and sway in perfect unison, getting faster and faster.
Dancers beat drums strapped to their bodies while they leap and spin, to honour ancestors during the summer Obon festival.
A bouncy "hop-step-close-step" partner dance from Bohemia that became a craze across Europe in the 1840s.
